questions.q: In Anglo-Saxon England, which system made groups of ten men responsible for each other's behaviour?
questions.explain: In the tithing, men over twelve were grouped to keep one another in order and report crimes.

questions.q: In the medieval period, 'trial by ordeal' was believed to reveal guilt through whose judgement?
questions.explain: Trial by ordeal assumed God would protect the innocent, for example by healing a burn cleanly.

questions.q: The 'Bloody Code' refers to what feature of 18th-century English justice?
options: The use of torture to extract confessions
The trial of the dead in court
The large number of crimes punishable by death
questions.explain: The Bloody Code listed over 200 crimes, even minor theft, as capital offences punishable by hanging.

questions.q: Public executions in Britain were abolished in which year, moving hangings inside prisons?
questions.explain: From 1868, executions were carried out privately within prison walls rather than before crowds.

questions.q: In which year was the Metropolitan Police force founded?
questions.explain: Sir Robert Peel established the Metropolitan Police in London in 1829.

questions.q: The Norman 'Forest Laws' chiefly made which activity a crime?
questions.explain: Forest Laws reserved hunting and timber in royal forests for the king, criminalising ordinary villagers.

questions.q: The 1888 Whitechapel murders were attributed to which unidentified killer?
questions.explain: The unsolved Whitechapel murders of 1888 were blamed on the figure known as Jack the Ripper.

questions.q: Which Home Secretary set up the Metropolitan Police, giving 'Peelers' and 'Bobbies' their nickname?
questions.explain: Robert Peel's 1829 reform gave the police their popular nicknames 'Peelers' and 'Bobbies'.

questions.q: Which feature of Whitechapel made policing especially difficult in the 1880s?
options: A lack of any local population
Overcrowded slums, poor lighting and narrow alleys
questions.explain: Whitechapel's dark, crowded slums and maze of alleys hampered detection and let suspects escape.

questions.q: In Tudor and Stuart England, accusations of which crime led to many trials and executions, especially of women?
questions.explain: Witchcraft was a serious crime in early-modern England, with peaks of trials during the 16th and 17th centuries.

questions.q: Vagabondage (begging and wandering without work) was treated as a serious crime mainly in which period?
questions.explain: Tudor laws punished 'sturdy beggars' and vagabonds harshly amid fears of disorder and unemployment.

questions.q: From the late 18th century, transportation usually meant sending convicts to where?
questions.explain: After American independence, convicts were transported to Australia from 1787 as an alternative to hanging.
